ctrl-001.title: Information Security Policy document
ctrl-001.description: A formal information security policy approved by management and communicated to all staff. Must cover scope, responsibilities, acceptable use, data classification, and incident response.

ctrl-002.title: Annual risk assessment process
ctrl-002.description: Regular risk assessments to identify threats, vulnerabilities, and impacts to critical services. Must use a recognized framework (ISO 27005, NIST).

ctrl-003.title: Risk register maintained and reviewed
ctrl-003.description: Active risk register tracking all identified cybersecurity risks with likelihood, impact, mitigation plans, and owners.

ctrl-004.title: Security roles and responsibilities defined
ctrl-004.description: Clear accountability with documented RACI matrix for security functions. Roles like CISO, security team, system owners must be formally defined.

ctrl-005.title: Incident response plan documented
ctrl-005.description: Formal incident response process covering detection, containment, eradication, recovery, and lessons learned. Must include escalation paths and communication templates.

ctrl-006.title: Incident classification and escalation process
ctrl-006.description: Defined severity levels (Critical, High, Medium, Low) with clear escalation criteria, response SLAs, and notification requirements.

ctrl-007.title: CSIRT registration completed
ctrl-007.description: Organization registered with national Computer Security Incident Response Team (CSIRT) for mandatory incident reporting.

ctrl-008.title: Incident response tabletop exercise conducted (last 12 months)
ctrl-008.description: Regular testing of incident response plan through tabletop exercises or simulations.

ctrl-009.title: 24-hour notification process to authorities defined
ctrl-009.description: Clear process for early warning notification to authorities within 24 hours of detecting a significant incident.

ctrl-010.title: Business continuity plan documented
ctrl-010.description: BCP ensuring critical services can continue during disruptions. Must cover critical functions, dependencies, alternate arrangements, and communication plans.

ctrl-011.title: Disaster recovery plan with RTO/RPO targets
ctrl-011.description: DR plan with defined Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) for each critical system.

ctrl-012.title: DR plan tested (last 12 months)
ctrl-012.description: Regular testing of disaster recovery plan through simulations or full failover tests.

ctrl-013.title: Critical system backups tested regularly
ctrl-013.description: Regular restore tests to verify backup integrity and restoration procedures. Quarterly testing required.

ctrl-014.title: Supplier cybersecurity assessment process
ctrl-014.description: Process to assess cybersecurity practices of critical suppliers, including security questionnaires and certification requirements.

ctrl-015.title: Security requirements in supplier contracts
ctrl-015.description: Contractual security obligations including breach notification, right to audit, data protection, and security certifications.

ctrl-016.title: Third-party access management process
ctrl-016.description: Formal approval, MFA enforcement, and monitoring for third-party system access. Quarterly access reviews required.

ctrl-017.title: MFA enabled on all critical systems
ctrl-017.description: Multi-factor authentication enforced on all critical systems, admin accounts, and remote access.

ctrl-018.title: Data encryption at rest and in transit
ctrl-018.description: Encryption of sensitive data using approved algorithms (AES-256, TLS 1.3) for data at rest and in transit.

ctrl-019.title: Network security monitoring in place
ctrl-019.description: Active monitoring of network traffic, intrusion detection, and security event logging.

ctrl-020.title: Vulnerability management process
ctrl-020.description: Regular vulnerability scanning, patch management, and remediation tracking for all systems.

ctrl-021.title: Cryptography and key management policy
ctrl-021.description: Policy governing encryption algorithms, key lifecycle, and secure key storage using KMS or HSM.

ctrl-022.title: Patch management process
ctrl-022.description: Systematic process for applying security patches to operating systems, applications, and firmware.

ctrl-023.title: Security awareness training completed by all staff
ctrl-023.description: Annual mandatory security awareness training covering phishing, password security, data handling, and incident reporting.

ctrl-024.title: Information security policy acknowledged by all staff
ctrl-024.description: All employees must read and formally acknowledge the information security policy annually.

ctrl-025.title: Secure onboarding process for new employees
ctrl-025.description: Security onboarding checklist including background checks, NDA signing, security training, and access provisioning.

ctrl-026.title: Same-day access revocation on employee departure
ctrl-026.description: Process ensuring all system access is disabled within 1 hour of employee departure. Equipment collection and exit interview.

ctrl-027.title: Privileged access background checks conducted
ctrl-027.description: Background verification for roles with admin rights or access to sensitive data (system admins, database admins, finance, HR).

ctrl-028.title: Annual access review completed
ctrl-028.description: Quarterly access certification where managers review and certify their team members' access rights.

ctrl-029.title: Management body approval of cybersecurity measures
ctrl-029.description: The management body has formally approved cybersecurity risk-management measures as required by NIS2 Article 20(1). Approval is documented in board minutes with coverage of risk appetite, cybersecurity strategy, budget allocation, and accountability structure. Approval must be renewed when significant changes occur or at minimum annually.

ctrl-030.title: Management body cybersecurity oversight and reporting
ctrl-030.description: The management body receives and reviews cybersecurity status reports at regular intervals (minimum quarterly) covering key risk metrics, recent incidents, compliance status, training completion rates, and emerging threats. This ensures ongoing board-level visibility and enables informed decision-making as required by NIS2 Article 20(1) oversight obligations.

ctrl-031.title: Management body cybersecurity training
ctrl-031.description: All management body members have completed cybersecurity training sufficient to identify risks, assess cybersecurity risk-management measures, and understand their impact on the entity's services. Training must be renewed annually and cover the current threat landscape, regulatory obligations, and board-level responsibilities. This is a mandatory requirement under NIS2 Article 20(2).

ctrl-032.title: Designated security leadership role
ctrl-032.description: A designated Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) or equivalent security leadership role is formally appointed with direct reporting to senior leadership or the management body. The role has clearly defined responsibilities, decision-making authority for cybersecurity matters, and a dedicated budget allocation.

ctrl-033.title: Security audit and penetration testing programme
ctrl-033.description: Regular security audits and penetration testing by qualified independent testers to validate that cybersecurity risk-management measures are effective. Tests must cover both external and internal attack surfaces of critical systems. All findings are documented with severity ratings and tracked through remediation to closure with re-testing. Implements NIS2 Article 21(2)(f) requirement to assess effectiveness of measures.

ctrl-034.title: Cybersecurity KPIs and metrics programme
ctrl-034.description: Defined cybersecurity key performance indicators (KPIs) are tracked regularly and reported to the management body to measure the effectiveness of risk-management measures. KPIs include both leading indicators (training completion, patch compliance, MFA coverage) and lagging indicators (incidents, mean time to detect, mean time to respond). Trends are analysed to drive continuous improvement.

ctrl-035.title: Audit and assessment finding remediation tracking
ctrl-035.description: All findings from security audits, penetration tests, risk assessments, and compliance reviews are logged in a central register with assigned owners, target remediation deadlines, and current status. Open findings are reviewed at least monthly. Overdue critical and high findings are escalated to management. Closure requires evidence of remediation and verification.

ctrl-036.title: Continuous improvement process
ctrl-036.description: A documented continuous improvement process ensures lessons learned from incidents, audits, penetration tests, threat intelligence, and regulatory changes are systematically fed back into policy updates, control improvements, and risk reassessments. This closes the feedback loop between effectiveness assessment and risk management, ensuring measures evolve with the threat landscape.

ctrl-037.title: Phishing simulation and response programme
ctrl-037.description: Regular simulated phishing campaigns are conducted at least quarterly to test employee awareness and measure real-world readiness. Click rates are tracked per campaign and per individual. Employees who repeatedly fail receive targeted additional training. Results and trends are reported to management to inform training priorities.

ctrl-038.title: Cyber hygiene baseline enforced
ctrl-038.description: Baseline cyber hygiene practices are documented in policy and enforced through technical controls where possible. Covers automatic software updates, screen lock timeouts (maximum 5 minutes), password manager usage, clean desk policy, and removable media restrictions. NIS2 Article 21(2)(g) explicitly requires basic cyber hygiene practices as a minimum measure.

ctrl-039.title: Data classification with encryption requirements
ctrl-039.description: A data classification scheme defines sensitivity levels (Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted) with corresponding encryption requirements per level. Classification guidance is provided to data owners for consistent application. The scheme is reviewed annually and updated when business or regulatory requirements change. Supports NIS2 Article 21(2)(h) requirement for cryptography policies.

ctrl-040.title: Continuous or adaptive authentication for high-risk access
ctrl-040.description: Continuous or adaptive authentication mechanisms adjust security requirements based on risk signals such as location, device posture, user behaviour, and time of access for high-risk scenarios. Legacy authentication protocols (NTLM, basic authentication) that bypass multi-factor authentication are blocked. NIS2 Article 21(2)(j) explicitly references continuous authentication solutions.

ctrl-041.title: Secured voice, video, and text communications
ctrl-041.description: End-to-end encrypted communication channels are approved and used for sensitive business communications including voice, video, and text. An approved tools list is maintained, communicated to all staff, and reviewed periodically. Tools are verified to provide end-to-end encryption. NIS2 Article 21(2)(j) explicitly requires secured voice, video and text communications.

ctrl-042.title: Secured emergency communication system
ctrl-042.description: A pre-established emergency communication system is operational and can function independently if primary communication channels are compromised during a cybersecurity incident. Contact lists are maintained and accessible offline. The system is tested during business continuity and incident response exercises. NIS2 Article 21(2)(j) explicitly requires secured emergency communication systems within the entity.

ctrl-043.title: MFA bypass prevention and monitoring
ctrl-043.description: Controls are in place to prevent and detect multi-factor authentication bypass attacks including MFA fatigue (push bombing), adversary-in-the-middle token theft, and SIM swap attacks. Push notification rate limiting is enabled. SMS-based MFA is deprecated in favour of phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO2 hardware tokens or passkeys. Monitoring alerts on MFA bypass attempts.

nis2-020-01.question: Has the management body formally approved the cybersecurity risk-management measures?
nis2-020-01.description: NIS2 Article 20 requires the management body to approve and oversee cybersecurity risk-management measures.
nis2-020-01.guidance: Present cybersecurity strategy to the board. Document approval in board minutes. Include risk appetite, budget, and KPIs.

nis2-020-02.question: Does the management body review cybersecurity status reports at least quarterly?
nis2-020-02.description: Regular board-level reporting ensures ongoing visibility of cybersecurity posture and emerging risks.
nis2-020-02.guidance: Produce quarterly dashboards: key metrics, recent incidents, compliance status, training completion, audit findings.

nis2-020-03.question: Have management body members completed cybersecurity training for their oversight role?
nis2-020-03.description: NIS2 mandates that management body members undertake training to gain sufficient knowledge and skills to identify risks.
nis2-020-03.guidance: Schedule annual executive cybersecurity briefings. Cover threat landscape, regulatory obligations, and board responsibilities.

nis2-020-04.question: Is there a designated CISO or equivalent with direct reporting to senior leadership?
nis2-020-04.description: Clear accountability requires a dedicated security leader with authority and visibility at the executive level.
nis2-020-04.guidance: Appoint a CISO or Head of Security reporting to CEO or board. Define responsibilities, authority, and budget in writing.

nis2-21a-01.question: Is there a formal information security policy reviewed at least annually?
nis2-21a-01.description: A documented IS policy is the foundation. It must be reviewed and updated to reflect changes in threats and business.
nis2-21a-01.guidance: Create or update IS policy covering scope, objectives, roles, acceptable use, classification, and review schedule.

nis2-21a-02.question: Is an annual risk assessment conducted using a recognised methodology (ISO 27005, NIST RMF)?
nis2-21a-02.description: Systematic risk assessment identifies and prioritises threats. A recognised framework ensures completeness.
nis2-21a-02.guidance: Adopt ISO 27005 or NIST RMF. Document assets, threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood, impact, and treatment plans.

nis2-21a-03.question: Are cybersecurity risks in the enterprise risk register with owners and treatment plans?
nis2-21a-03.description: Cyber risks must be integrated into enterprise risk management, not siloed in IT.
nis2-21a-03.guidance: Add cyber risks to the enterprise risk register. Score by likelihood and impact. Assign owners. Review quarterly.

nis2-21a-04.question: Are security roles and responsibilities clearly defined and communicated (RACI matrix)?
nis2-21a-04.description: Clear ownership prevents gaps. A RACI matrix maps who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed.
nis2-21a-04.guidance: Create a security RACI matrix. Communicate roles during onboarding and annual policy reviews.

nis2-21b-01.question: Is there a documented incident response plan covering detection through lessons learned?
nis2-21b-01.description: A complete IRP covers preparation, detection, containment, eradication, recovery, and post-incident review.
nis2-21b-01.guidance: Document IRP with phases, roles, communication templates, and escalation paths. Test annually.

nis2-21b-02.question: Are incident severity levels defined with escalation paths and response SLAs?
nis2-21b-02.description: Classification ensures proportionate response. SLAs set expectations for triage and resolution.
nis2-21b-02.guidance: Define severity levels (P1-P4). Map escalation paths. Set SLAs: P1 within 1 hour, P2 within 4 hours.

nis2-21b-03.question: Are you registered with your national CSIRT and have you tested the 24-hour notification process?
nis2-21b-03.description: NIS2 requires early warning to the CSIRT within 24 hours of a significant incident.
nis2-21b-03.guidance: Register with national CSIRT. Document notification process. Run a tabletop exercise testing 24h notification.

nis2-21b-04.question: Is there an incident register documenting all events, investigations, and post-incident reviews?
nis2-21b-04.description: A register demonstrates accountability, enables trend analysis, and supports regulatory reporting.
nis2-21b-04.guidance: Use a ticketing system to log all incidents. Record: date, reporter, severity, investigation, resolution, lessons learned.

nis2-21b-05.question: Has the incident response plan been tested through tabletop exercises or simulations in the last 12 months?
nis2-21b-05.description: An untested IRP may fail under pressure. Regular testing validates procedures, roles, and communication flows.
nis2-21b-05.guidance: Conduct at least annual tabletop exercises simulating realistic scenarios. Include cross-functional teams. Document findings and update the IRP.

nis2-21c-01.question: Is there a documented BCP identifying critical functions, dependencies, and recovery priorities?
nis2-21c-01.description: A BCP ensures the organisation can maintain essential operations during and after a disruption.
nis2-21c-01.guidance: Conduct BIA to identify critical functions. Document dependencies, recovery priorities, and communication plans.

nis2-21c-02.question: Are there DR plans with defined RTO/RPO for all critical systems?
nis2-21c-02.description: Recovery Time Objective and Recovery Point Objective define acceptable downtime and data loss.
nis2-21c-02.guidance: Define RTO/RPO per critical system. Document DR procedures including failover steps and responsible teams.

nis2-21c-03.question: Have BCP/DR plans been tested in the last 12 months (tabletop, simulation, or failover)?
nis2-21c-03.description: Untested plans may fail when needed. Regular testing validates procedures and builds muscle memory.
nis2-21c-03.guidance: Schedule annual BCP/DR tests. Start with tabletop exercises, progress to full failover tests for critical systems.

nis2-21c-04.question: Are backup restorations tested regularly and backup integrity verified?
nis2-21c-04.description: Backups are only useful if they can be restored. Regular testing verifies data integrity and recovery procedures.
nis2-21c-04.guidance: Test backup restoration monthly for critical systems. Verify data integrity. Document results and remediate failures.

nis2-21c-05.question: Is there a crisis communication plan covering internal notification, regulatory reporting, and media handling?
nis2-21c-05.description: During a crisis, clear communication is critical. Delays or misinformation worsen impact and may violate NIS2 notification requirements.
nis2-21c-05.guidance: Document communication templates, spokesperson designation, notification chains, and media handling procedures. Test during BCP exercises.

nis2-21d-01.question: Is there a formal process for assessing supplier cybersecurity posture?
nis2-21d-01.description: Supply chain attacks are a primary vector. Assessing suppliers before engagement reduces third-party risk.
nis2-21d-01.guidance: Require vendors to complete security questionnaires. Review SOC 2/ISO 27001 reports. Assess annually.

nis2-21d-02.question: Do contracts include NIS2-aligned security obligations (breach notification, audit rights)?
nis2-21d-02.description: Contractual obligations ensure suppliers maintain security standards and notify you of incidents.
nis2-21d-02.guidance: Add contract clauses: breach notification within 24h, right to audit, insurance, data residency, subprocessor approval.

nis2-21d-03.question: Is there a register of third-party integrations, access levels, and data processed?
nis2-21d-03.description: You cannot protect what you do not know. A complete register enables risk assessment and access control.
nis2-21d-03.guidance: Inventory all SaaS tools, APIs, vendor connections. Document: data accessed, owner, contract details, review date.

nis2-21d-04.question: Does third-party access require approval, MFA, time limits, and monitoring?
nis2-21d-04.description: Uncontrolled vendor access is a common breach vector. Strict controls limit exposure.
nis2-21d-04.guidance: Require formal approval for vendor access. Enforce MFA, set time-limited sessions, enable audit logging.

nis2-21e-01.question: Is there a formal vulnerability management policy with remediation timelines?
nis2-21e-01.description: A policy defines how vulnerabilities are identified, assessed, prioritised, and remediated within set timelines.
nis2-21e-01.guidance: Define remediation SLAs: Critical 24h, High 7d, Medium 30d, Low 90d. Track compliance. Use CVSS for scoring.

nis2-21e-02.question: Are security requirements verified during system acquisition, development, and maintenance?
nis2-21e-02.description: Security must be embedded in the SDLC, not bolted on. Requirements should be verified at each stage.
nis2-21e-02.guidance: Integrate security gates in SDLC: threat modelling, secure code review, SAST/DAST, penetration testing before release.

nis2-21e-03.question: Is there a responsible vulnerability disclosure process and dependency monitoring?
nis2-21e-03.description: A disclosure process handles reported vulnerabilities. Dependency monitoring catches known CVEs in libraries.
nis2-21e-03.guidance: Publish a security.txt / vulnerability disclosure policy. Monitor dependencies with Dependabot/Snyk. Review weekly.

nis2-21e-04.question: Are critical/high vulnerabilities remediated within defined SLAs?
nis2-21e-04.description: Identifying vulnerabilities is only useful if they are fixed. SLA compliance demonstrates operational maturity.
nis2-21e-04.guidance: Track SLA compliance metrics. Escalate overdue critical/high vulnerabilities to management. Report monthly.

nis2-21e-05.question: Are automated security scanning tools (SAST, DAST, dependency scanning) integrated into the CI/CD pipeline?
nis2-21e-05.description: Manual security reviews do not scale. Automated scanning catches common vulnerabilities early and consistently.
nis2-21e-05.guidance: Integrate SAST (e.g. SonarQube, Semgrep) and dependency scanning (Dependabot, Snyk) into CI/CD. Fail builds on critical findings.

nis2-21f-01.question: Are controls tested via audits, penetration tests, or red team exercises?
nis2-21f-01.description: Testing validates that controls work as intended. Without testing, compliance is theoretical.
nis2-21f-01.guidance: Conduct annual penetration tests. Perform internal audits quarterly. Consider red team exercises for critical systems.

nis2-21f-02.question: Are cybersecurity KPIs tracked (MTTD, MTTR, patch compliance, etc.)?
nis2-21f-02.description: KPIs provide objective measurement of security posture and identify areas needing improvement.
nis2-21f-02.guidance: Track: MTTD, MTTR, patch compliance rate, phishing click rate, training completion, open vulnerabilities count.

nis2-21f-03.question: Are audit findings tracked to remediation with owners and deadlines?
nis2-21f-03.description: Audit findings without follow-up provide no value. Tracking ensures accountability and closure.
nis2-21f-03.guidance: Log all audit findings in a tracker. Assign owners and deadlines. Review progress monthly. Escalate overdue items.

nis2-21f-04.question: Does a continuous improvement process feed audit/incident/threat intel into policy updates?
nis2-21f-04.description: Lessons learned should drive policy and control improvements. This closes the feedback loop.
nis2-21f-04.guidance: After audits and major incidents, update relevant policies and controls. Document changes and rationale.

nis2-21g-01.question: Is mandatory security training provided on hire and renewed annually?
nis2-21g-01.description: All staff must receive baseline security training. Annual renewal keeps knowledge current.
nis2-21g-01.guidance: Implement onboarding training covering: password policies, MFA, phishing, data handling, incident reporting. Renew yearly.

nis2-21g-02.question: Are phishing simulations conducted at least quarterly with results tracked?
nis2-21g-02.description: Simulated campaigns measure real-world readiness and identify individuals needing additional training.
nis2-21g-02.guidance: Run quarterly phishing simulations. Provide immediate feedback to clickers. Track metrics and trends over time.

nis2-21g-03.question: Is role-specific security training provided for technical staff?
nis2-21g-03.description: Engineers and admins need specialised training beyond general awareness (secure coding, cloud security).
nis2-21g-03.guidance: Provide training: Developers (OWASP, secure coding), Admins (least privilege, logging), Cloud engineers (IAM, encryption).

nis2-21g-04.question: Are cyber hygiene requirements documented and enforced (updates, screen lock, passwords)?
nis2-21g-04.description: Basic hygiene practices reduce the attack surface. They must be documented and enforced, not just recommended.
nis2-21g-04.guidance: Document hygiene requirements: auto-updates enabled, screen lock after 5 min, password manager required, clean desk policy.

nis2-21h-01.question: Is there a formal cryptography policy specifying approved algorithms and minimum key lengths?
nis2-21h-01.description: A cryptography policy prevents use of weak or deprecated algorithms and ensures consistent standards.
nis2-21h-01.guidance: Define approved algorithms (AES-256, RSA-2048+, SHA-256+). Ban deprecated algorithms. Review annually.

nis2-21h-02.question: Is there a key management lifecycle covering generation, rotation, revocation, and destruction?
nis2-21h-02.description: Poor key management undermines encryption. Keys must be properly managed throughout their lifecycle.
nis2-21h-02.guidance: Document key management procedures. Use HSMs for critical keys. Rotate keys per policy. Securely destroy retired keys.

nis2-21h-03.question: Is data classified with encryption requirements defined per classification level?
nis2-21h-03.description: Not all data needs the same protection. Classification drives proportionate encryption controls.
nis2-21h-03.guidance: Define data classification levels (Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted). Map encryption requirements per level.

nis2-21h-04.question: Is encryption enforced at rest and in transit, with TLS 1.2+ for external communications?
nis2-21h-04.description: Data must be protected both at rest (disk/database) and in transit (network). TLS 1.2 is the minimum standard.
nis2-21h-04.guidance: Enable encryption at rest for all databases and storage. Enforce TLS 1.2+ for all external connections. Disable TLS 1.0/1.1.

nis2-21i-01.question: Is there an access control policy with least privilege, RBAC, and quarterly reviews?
nis2-21i-01.description: Access control is foundational. Least privilege limits blast radius; RBAC simplifies management; reviews catch drift.
nis2-21i-01.guidance: Document RBAC model, approval workflows, review schedule. Conduct quarterly access reviews. Remove unused access.

nis2-21i-02.question: Does onboarding include security training, NDA, and role-based provisioning before access?
nis2-21i-02.description: Consistent onboarding prevents gaps. Training and legal agreements must precede system access.
nis2-21i-02.guidance: Onboarding checklist: NDA signed, security training completed, role-based access provisioned, hardware issued.

nis2-21i-03.question: Is there same-day account revocation on departure with a formal offboarding checklist?
nis2-21i-03.description: Delayed offboarding creates risk. Departing employees must lose access immediately.
nis2-21i-03.guidance: HR notifies IT same-day. Disable accounts within 1 hour. Revoke: email, VPN, SSO, cloud services, physical badges.

nis2-21i-04.question: Is there an asset inventory (hardware, software, data) with owners and classification?
nis2-21i-04.description: You cannot protect what you do not know. A complete asset inventory is the basis for risk management.
nis2-21i-04.guidance: Maintain inventory of all hardware, software, and data assets. Assign owners. Classify by sensitivity. Review quarterly.

nis2-21i-05.question: Is privileged access managed with additional controls (PAM, time-limited sessions, enhanced logging)?
nis2-21i-05.description: Privileged accounts are prime targets for attackers. Standard access controls are insufficient for admin-level access.
nis2-21i-05.guidance: Implement PAM solution. Require just-in-time access for admin tasks. Log all privileged sessions. Review privileged access monthly.

nis2-21i-06.question: Are background or security checks performed for personnel in roles with elevated access?
nis2-21i-06.description: Personnel with privileged access or handling sensitive data pose higher risk. Pre-employment screening reduces insider threat.
nis2-21i-06.guidance: Perform background checks for privileged roles before granting access. Define which roles require checks. Review policy annually.

nis2-21j-01.question: Is MFA enforced for critical systems using hardware tokens or authenticator apps (not SMS)?
nis2-21j-01.description: SMS-based MFA is vulnerable to SIM-swap attacks. Hardware tokens or authenticator apps are required.
nis2-21j-01.guidance: Enforce MFA for all critical systems. Use hardware tokens (FIDO2/U2F) or authenticator apps. Block SMS-based MFA.

nis2-21j-02.question: Are end-to-end encrypted channels used for sensitive voice, video, and text communications?
nis2-21j-02.description: Sensitive communications must be protected from eavesdropping with end-to-end encryption.
nis2-21j-02.guidance: Use E2E encrypted tools for sensitive comms (Signal, Teams with E2E, encrypted email). Document approved channels.

nis2-21j-03.question: Are secured emergency communications operational if primary systems are compromised?
nis2-21j-03.description: If primary comms are down during an incident, you need a backup channel that is pre-established and tested.
nis2-21j-03.guidance: Establish out-of-band comms (separate messaging app, satellite phone, personal devices). Test during DR exercises.

nis2-21j-04.question: Is legacy authentication blocked and continuous/adaptive auth used for high-risk access?
nis2-21j-04.description: Legacy auth protocols bypass MFA. Adaptive auth adjusts requirements based on risk signals.
nis2-21j-04.guidance: Block legacy auth (NTLM, basic auth). Implement conditional access policies. Use adaptive MFA for high-risk logins.

tpl-isp.title: Information Security Policy
tpl-isp.summary1: You are responsible for protecting company data, systems, and information assets at all times.
tpl-isp.summary2: All sensitive data must be classified and handled according to its classification level (Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted).
tpl-isp.summary3: Passwords must meet minimum complexity requirements and must never be shared with anyone, including IT staff.
tpl-isp.summary4: All security incidents, suspected breaches, or policy violations must be reported to the IT security team immediately.
tpl-isp.summary5: Access to systems and data is granted on a need-to-know, least-privilege basis and is subject to periodic review.
tpl-isp.summary6: Personal devices used for work must comply with company security standards including encryption and screen lock.
tpl-isp.summary7: Violations of this policy may result in disciplinary action, up to and including termination, and may also carry legal consequences under NIS2.

tpl-aup.title: Acceptable Use Policy
tpl-aup.summary1: Company IT resources (email, internet, devices, cloud services) are provided for business purposes and limited personal use.
tpl-aup.summary2: You must not install unauthorised software, disable security tools, or attempt to bypass access controls on any company system.
tpl-aup.summary3: Company email must not be used for personal financial transactions, chain letters, or any communication that could harm the organisation's reputation.
tpl-aup.summary4: Internet usage is monitored for security purposes. Accessing illegal, offensive, or malicious content is strictly prohibited.
tpl-aup.summary5: Removable media (USB drives, external hard drives) must not be connected to company systems without prior approval from IT security.
tpl-aup.summary6: You must lock your workstation whenever you leave it unattended, even for short periods. Screen lock must activate within 5 minutes of inactivity.

tpl-irp.title: Incident Response Policy
tpl-irp.summary1: A security incident is any event that compromises or threatens the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of company data or systems.
tpl-irp.summary2: If you suspect a security incident (phishing, unauthorised access, data leak, malware), report it immediately to the IT security team — do not attempt to investigate yourself.
tpl-irp.summary3: Incidents are classified by severity: Critical (immediate business impact), High (significant risk), Medium (limited impact), Low (minor issue).
tpl-irp.summary4: Under NIS2, significant incidents must be reported to national authorities within 24 hours. Delays in internal reporting can prevent timely notification.
tpl-irp.summary5: Do not delete, modify, or destroy any evidence related to a security incident. Preserve logs, emails, screenshots, and affected systems.
tpl-irp.summary6: After an incident is resolved, a post-incident review will identify root causes and improvements. Your cooperation in these reviews is mandatory.

tpl-bcp.title: Business Continuity Policy
tpl-bcp.summary1: Critical business functions have been identified and prioritised. Your role may be classified as critical — check with your manager if you are unsure.
tpl-bcp.summary2: If primary systems become unavailable, follow the documented alternate procedures for your department. These are available on the company intranet.
tpl-bcp.summary3: In a major disruption, communication will be coordinated through the designated emergency communication channels. Ensure your contact details are up to date.
tpl-bcp.summary4: Recovery Time Objectives (RTO) and Recovery Point Objectives (RPO) have been defined for all critical systems. Compliance with these targets is mandatory.
tpl-bcp.summary5: Business continuity and disaster recovery plans are tested at least annually. You may be required to participate in exercises and simulations.
tpl-bcp.summary6: If you identify a situation that could disrupt critical services, report it immediately to your manager and the IT security team.

tpl-acc.title: Access Control and Identity Management Policy
tpl-acc.summary1: Access to systems and data is granted based on the principle of least privilege — you receive only the minimum access required for your role.
tpl-acc.summary2: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is mandatory for all critical systems. Never share your MFA tokens, codes, or hardware keys with anyone.
tpl-acc.summary3: When you change roles or responsibilities, your access rights will be reviewed and adjusted. Report any access you no longer need.
tpl-acc.summary4: All access rights are reviewed quarterly by managers. You may be asked to confirm that your current access levels are still appropriate.
tpl-acc.summary5: Upon leaving the organisation, all system access will be revoked within 1 hour. Return all company devices and access tokens on your last day.
tpl-acc.summary6: Sharing credentials, using another person's account, or allowing others to use your account is strictly prohibited.
tpl-acc.summary7: Privileged access (admin rights) requires additional controls including enhanced logging, time-limited sessions, and background verification.

tpl-sup.title: Supply Chain and Third-Party Security Policy
tpl-sup.summary1: All third-party vendors with access to company systems or data must pass a cybersecurity assessment before engagement.
tpl-sup.summary2: Vendor contracts must include security obligations: breach notification within 24 hours, right to audit, data protection requirements, and security certifications.
tpl-sup.summary3: Third-party system access requires formal approval, MFA enforcement, and is subject to monitoring and quarterly reviews.
tpl-sup.summary4: You must not share company credentials, system access, or sensitive data with any third party without prior written approval from IT security.
tpl-sup.summary5: Maintain an inventory of all third-party tools, integrations, and services used in your department. Report new tools to IT security before deployment.
tpl-sup.summary6: If a vendor reports a security incident or you suspect a third party has been compromised, report it immediately to the IT security team.

tpl-enc.title: Data Protection and Encryption Policy
tpl-enc.summary1: All sensitive data must be encrypted at rest (stored on disk) and in transit (sent over networks) using approved algorithms (AES-256, TLS 1.3).
tpl-enc.summary2: Data must be classified before storage or transmission: Public, Internal, Confidential, or Restricted. Encryption requirements increase with classification level.
tpl-enc.summary3: Encryption keys must be stored securely in approved key management systems (KMS/HSM). Never store encryption keys alongside the data they protect.
tpl-enc.summary4: Sending Confidential or Restricted data via unencrypted email, messaging apps, or file-sharing services is prohibited unless approved encrypted channels are used.
tpl-enc.summary5: All portable devices (laptops, phones, USB drives) containing company data must have full-disk encryption enabled.
tpl-enc.summary6: If you discover unencrypted sensitive data, or suspect an encryption failure, report it immediately to the IT security team.

tpl-hyg.title: Cyber Hygiene and Security Awareness Policy
tpl-hyg.summary1: All employees must complete annual security awareness training. New employees must complete training within their first week.
tpl-hyg.summary2: Keep all software and operating systems up to date. Enable automatic updates where available. Do not delay or defer security patches.
tpl-hyg.summary3: Use the company-approved password manager for all work accounts. Passwords must be unique per service — never reuse passwords across systems.
tpl-hyg.summary4: Be vigilant about phishing: verify sender addresses, do not click suspicious links, and report all suspected phishing emails to IT security.
tpl-hyg.summary5: Follow the clean desk policy: lock away sensitive documents when leaving your desk. Do not leave printed materials containing sensitive information unattended.
tpl-hyg.summary6: Removable media (USB drives, external disks) are restricted. Use only company-approved devices and scan for malware before use.
tpl-hyg.summary7: The organisation conducts regular phishing simulations. Employees who repeatedly fail simulations will receive targeted additional training.

quiz-001.question: What should you do if you receive a suspicious email with an unexpected attachment?
quiz-001.option1: Open the attachment to check if it is legitimate
quiz-001.option2: Forward it to colleagues to ask their opinion
quiz-001.option3: Report it to the IT security team without opening it
quiz-001.option4: Delete it and forget about it
quiz-001.explanation: Reporting suspicious emails to the IT security team allows them to investigate and protect the entire organisation. Never open unexpected attachments.

quiz-002.question: What is the safest way to manage your work passwords?
quiz-002.option1: Use the same password for all work accounts for convenience
quiz-002.option2: Use a unique strong password for each account and store them in an approved password manager
quiz-002.option3: Write them on a sticky note and keep it near your screen
quiz-002.option4: Share them with your manager so they can access your accounts if needed
quiz-002.explanation: Unique strong passwords stored in an approved password manager prevent credential stuffing attacks and limit the impact if one account is compromised.

quiz-003.question: What is phishing?
quiz-003.option1: A type of network performance issue caused by high traffic
quiz-003.option2: An attack that tricks people into revealing credentials or clicking malicious links
quiz-003.option3: A method for testing firewall configurations
quiz-003.option4: A type of antivirus software used for email scanning
quiz-003.explanation: Phishing is the most common cyber attack vector. Attackers impersonate trusted entities to steal credentials, install malware, or gain access to systems.

quiz-004.question: What should you do when leaving your workstation, even briefly?
quiz-004.option1: Leave everything open — you will be right back
quiz-004.option2: Ask a colleague to watch your screen
quiz-004.option4: Turn off the monitor but leave the session open
quiz-004.explanation: Locking your screen (Win+L or Cmd+Ctrl+Q) takes seconds and prevents unauthorised access to your session, email, and sensitive data.

quiz-005.question: Who should you contact first if you suspect a security incident?
quiz-005.option1: The IT security team or your direct manager
quiz-005.option2: Your personal IT contact outside the company
quiz-005.option3: No one — try to fix it yourself first
quiz-005.option4: Post about it on social media to warn others
quiz-005.explanation: Fast reporting to the IT security team minimises damage. Under NIS2, organisations must report significant incidents to authorities within 24 hours.

quiz-006.question: Under NIS2, how quickly must a significant security incident be reported to the national authority?
quiz-006.option2: Within 24 hours (early warning) and 72 hours (full notification)
quiz-006.option4: Only if the incident results in financial loss
quiz-006.explanation: NIS2 Article 23 requires an early warning within 24 hours and a detailed notification within 72 hours of becoming aware of a significant incident.

quiz-007.question: What is the correct order of steps in an incident response process?
quiz-007.explanation: The standard incident response lifecycle is: Detection and analysis, Containment, Eradication and Recovery, then Post-incident review (lessons learned).

quiz-008.question: What should be included in an incident report?
quiz-008.option1: Only the name of the person who caused the incident
quiz-008.option2: A brief one-line summary with no technical detail
quiz-008.option3: Date, description, affected systems, actions taken, and impact assessment
quiz-008.option4: Only the financial cost of the incident
quiz-008.explanation: A thorough incident report enables root cause analysis, supports NIS2 compliance requirements, and helps prevent similar incidents in the future.

quiz-009.question: What does the principle of least privilege mean?
quiz-009.option1: Users should only have the minimum access rights needed for their job function
quiz-009.option2: Only senior managers should have access to IT systems
quiz-009.option3: Everyone should have full admin access to avoid bottlenecks
quiz-009.option4: Access rights should only be reviewed when someone leaves the company
quiz-009.explanation: Least privilege limits the blast radius if an account is compromised and reduces the risk of accidental data exposure or modification.

quiz-010.question: Why is Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) important?
quiz-010.option1: It makes logins faster and more convenient
quiz-010.option2: It replaces the need for strong passwords
quiz-010.option3: It is only required for IT administrators
quiz-010.option4: It adds an extra layer of security beyond passwords, making compromised credentials less useful to attackers
quiz-010.explanation: MFA ensures that stolen passwords alone cannot grant access. NIS2 expects organisations to implement strong authentication for critical systems.

quiz-011.question: What should happen when an employee changes roles within the organisation?
quiz-011.option1: Their access rights remain the same since they are still an employee
quiz-011.option2: Their access rights should be reviewed and adjusted to match their new role
quiz-011.option3: They should receive additional access on top of their existing permissions
quiz-011.option4: Access reviews only happen annually, so no action is needed immediately
quiz-011.explanation: Role changes require prompt access review to prevent privilege creep. Users should only retain permissions needed for their current responsibilities.

quiz-012.question: What is the recommended action when an employee leaves the organisation?
quiz-012.option1: Disable all accounts and revoke access immediately on the last working day
quiz-012.option2: Leave accounts active for 30 days in case they return
quiz-012.option3: Only disable email — other systems can wait
quiz-012.option4: Transfer their credentials to their replacement
quiz-012.explanation: Immediate account deactivation prevents former employees from accessing systems. This includes VPN, cloud services, email, and physical access.

quiz-013.question: What is the correct way to handle confidential documents you no longer need?
quiz-013.option1: Throw them in the regular office bin
quiz-013.option2: Leave them on your desk for the cleaning crew
quiz-013.option3: Use a cross-cut shredder or secure disposal bin
quiz-013.option4: Take them home for personal records
quiz-013.explanation: Confidential documents must be securely destroyed to prevent data leakage. Cross-cut shredding or secure disposal services are required under data protection rules.

quiz-014.question: When is encryption required for data transmission?
quiz-014.option1: Only when sending data to external partners
quiz-014.option2: Whenever sensitive or confidential data is transmitted, whether internally or externally
quiz-014.option3: Only when specifically requested by the recipient
quiz-014.option4: Encryption is optional and only recommended for financial data
quiz-014.explanation: NIS2 requires appropriate encryption for data in transit. All sensitive data transmissions should use TLS/HTTPS or equivalent encryption.

quiz-015.question: Which of the following is a good practice for data classification?
quiz-015.option1: Classify all data as confidential to be safe
quiz-015.option2: Only classify data that is stored in the cloud
quiz-015.option3: Let each employee decide how to classify their own data
quiz-015.option4: Apply classification levels (Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted) based on the sensitivity and impact of disclosure
quiz-015.explanation: Proper classification ensures that appropriate security controls are applied proportionally. Over-classification wastes resources; under-classification creates risk.

quiz-016.question: What should you do if you accidentally send sensitive data to the wrong recipient?
quiz-016.option1: Notify your manager and the IT security team immediately
quiz-016.option2: Send a follow-up email asking them to delete it
quiz-016.option4: Wait to see if the recipient notices
quiz-016.explanation: Accidental data exposure is a security incident that must be reported. Quick action allows the organisation to assess impact and take corrective measures.

quiz-017.question: Why is supply chain security important under NIS2?
quiz-017.option1: It only matters for manufacturing companies
quiz-017.option2: NIS2 does not address supply chain security
quiz-017.option3: A breach at a supplier can compromise your organisation, and NIS2 requires managing third-party risks
quiz-017.option4: It is important only if suppliers have physical access to your offices
quiz-017.explanation: NIS2 Article 21(2)(d) explicitly requires supply chain security measures. High-profile breaches (SolarWinds, Kaseya) have shown that supplier compromises can cascade.

quiz-018.question: What should you verify before granting a third-party vendor access to your systems?
quiz-018.option1: That they have completed a security assessment and have appropriate security controls in place
quiz-018.option2: That they are a well-known brand
quiz-018.option3: That they have been a vendor for more than a year
quiz-018.option4: Nothing special — if management approved them, that is sufficient
quiz-018.explanation: Vendor risk assessments should evaluate security certifications (ISO 27001, SOC 2), security policies, incident response capabilities, and data handling practices.

quiz-019.question: What is a key requirement for contracts with critical ICT service providers under NIS2?
quiz-019.option1: They must be renewed annually regardless of performance
quiz-019.option2: They must include security obligations, breach notification requirements, and audit rights
quiz-019.option3: They must be signed by the national cybersecurity authority
quiz-019.option4: They only need standard commercial terms
quiz-019.explanation: NIS2 requires that contracts with critical suppliers include specific security provisions, incident notification clauses, and the right to audit their security posture.

quiz-020.question: How should you handle a situation where a third-party vendor reports a data breach affecting your data?
quiz-020.option1: Wait for the vendor to resolve it completely before taking action
quiz-020.option3: Ignore it if the vendor says the impact is minimal
quiz-020.option4: Activate your incident response process, assess the impact on your organisation, and notify authorities if required
quiz-020.explanation: A vendor breach affecting your data is your incident too. You must assess the impact, invoke your incident response plan, and meet NIS2 notification deadlines.

quiz-021.question: What is the primary purpose of a Business Continuity Plan (BCP)?
quiz-021.option1: To document the company's financial performance
quiz-021.option2: To ensure critical business functions can continue during and after a disruption
quiz-021.option3: To list all employees and their contact information
quiz-021.option4: To satisfy auditors with documentation only
quiz-021.explanation: A BCP ensures that essential services remain available during crises. NIS2 Article 21(2)(c) requires business continuity and crisis management measures.

quiz-022.question: How often should backup restoration be tested?
quiz-022.option1: Regularly, at least quarterly, to verify that backups can be successfully restored
quiz-022.option2: Only when a real disaster occurs
quiz-022.option3: Once when the backup system is first set up
quiz-022.option4: Testing is not necessary if backups are automated
quiz-022.explanation: Untested backups may fail when needed most. Regular restoration tests verify data integrity and ensure that recovery time objectives can actually be met.

quiz-023.question: What is a Recovery Time Objective (RTO)?
quiz-023.option1: The amount of time it takes to detect an incident
quiz-023.option2: The total cost of recovering from a disaster
quiz-023.option3: The maximum acceptable time to restore a system or service after a disruption
quiz-023.option4: The number of staff needed for disaster recovery
quiz-023.explanation: RTO defines how quickly a system must be restored. It drives decisions about backup strategies, redundancy, and disaster recovery infrastructure.

quiz-024.question: What role does crisis communication play in business continuity?
quiz-024.option1: It is only important for the PR department
quiz-024.option2: It is optional and only needed for public-facing incidents
quiz-024.option3: It is handled automatically by IT systems
quiz-024.option4: It ensures stakeholders, employees, and authorities are informed promptly and accurately during a disruption
quiz-024.explanation: Clear crisis communication reduces confusion, maintains trust, and meets NIS2 requirements for timely notification of affected parties and authorities.
